recent_cases.parties: Robert Palmer v Keramos Pty Ltd
recent_cases.ai_summary: Mr Palmer filed an unfair dismissal application more than 21 days after dismissal and was directed to file materials supporting an extension of time. He failed to comply with the directions despite multiple reminders and opportunities, so Keramos applied under s399A to have the application dismissed. The Commission found he unreasonably failed to comply with directions and dismissed the application.

The applicant, employed by a labour hire provider (Zoom) and placed with Elgas on a casual assignment, alleged disability discrimination after her request for a temporary work-from-home arrangement was refused and her assignment terminated. She sought leave under s 46PO(3A)(a) of the AHRC Act to bring proceedings against Zoom, contending Zoom was directly involved in and managed her request for a reasonable adjustment. The Federal Court found the claim reasonably arguable, with intertwined factual issues requiring trial, and granted leave, referring the matter to mediation.

The Fair Work Ombudsman brought proceedings against the sole director of a restaurant company for underpayment of penalty rates, overtime, split shift allowances, annual leave and leave loading, and record-keeping failures. The director failed to file a defence, comply with Court orders or attend hearings, so the Court granted default judgment under r 5.23, treating the pleaded facts as admitted. The Court declared contraventions, ordered compensation and interest, and listed the matter for a penalty hearing.

Mr Daliwan filed an unfair dismissal application one day late after being dismissed by HammondCare for locking a violent dementia resident outside a cottage. The Commission found no acceptable reason for the delay, that he was aware of the dismissal when it took effect, took no action to dispute it, and had limited prospects of success on the merits. The extension of time was refused.

recent_cases.parties: Mr Albertus Neethling v SC Hydro Pty Ltd
recent_cases.ai_summary: Following an earlier finding that Mr Neethling's dismissal by SC Hydro was harsh, unjust and unreasonable and that reinstatement was inappropriate, the Commission determined compensation. Applying the Sprigg formula, the Deputy President assessed remuneration lost, deducted post-termination earnings, accounted for the applicant's failure to mitigate his loss, and applied a 10% reduction for misconduct that contributed to the dismissal. Compensation of $60,417.85 gross plus superannuation was ordered in lieu of reinstatement.
